exercises.title: Reading a Global Variable
description: Read an integer into a variable called LIMIT at the
top level of the program. Define a function show_limit()
that prints LIMIT, and call it.
<pre>> python program.py
A variable defined outside of any function — at the
top level of the file — is called a global
variable. Any function can freely read a global variable
without any special syntax.

exercises.title: A Global Constant
description: Using the fixed global MAX_SCORE = 100, define a
function cap_score(score) that returns
MAX_SCORE if score is higher than it,
or score unchanged otherwise. Read a score, call the
function, and print the result.
<pre>> python program.py
Writing a global's name in ALL_CAPS is a common
Python convention — it signals to anyone reading the code
"this value is meant to stay constant," even though Python itself
doesn't actually enforce that.

exercises.title: Modifying a Global with global
description: Starting from score = 0, define
add_points(points) that adds points to
the global score. Read a number, call the function,
and print score afterward.
<pre>> python program.py
5
To actually change a global variable from inside a
function (not just read it), you need to tell Python that's what
you mean, with a global score line at the top of the
function — otherwise, an assignment inside a function only
affects a variable local to that function.

exercises.title: A Counter Across Multiple Calls

increment() that adds 1 to the global
count each time it's called. Read a number
n, call increment() that many times in a
loop, then print the final count.
<pre>> python program.py

This is what makes globals genuinely useful sometimes: several
separate calls to the same function, all quietly updating one
shared value.

exercises.title: Fix the Bug: Forgetting global Entirely
description: This code is supposed to add 5 points to a global score and print
the result. Run it and read the error message closely.
Because score is assigned to somewhere inside
add_points, Python treats score as a
local variable for the function's entire body
— including the score + points part, which runs
before that local score has ever been given a
value. The fix is the same one from a couple of exercises ago: add
global score at the top of the function.

exercises.title: Preferring Parameters Over Globals
description: Rewrite the running-total idea from a couple of exercises ago,
but without using any global variable at all.
Define add(total, n) and
subtract(total, n), each taking the current total as a
parameter and returning the new total, rather than
modifying anything global. Read two numbers and print the final
result.
<pre>> python program.py
7
Globals can be convenient, but passing values in and returning
results out is usually easier to follow and to test — there's
no hidden shared state to keep track of, since everything a
function needs comes in through its parameters.

exercises.title: Fix the Bug: Silent Shadowing
description: This code is supposed to set a global score to whatever value is
read from input, and then print it. Run it and see what actually
happens — notice that unlike the earlier bug in this unit,
there's no error at all here.
Since set_score never declares global
score, the line score = points quietly creates
a brand new local variable that just happens to
share a name with the global one. The function runs perfectly
fine and even "succeeds" internally — it just never touches
the actual global score at all, which is why it's
still 0 afterward, no matter what value was passed in.
